Overflowing
o-ver-FLO-ing
a. & n.
From over and flow: to run over the brim or bank. Webster 1828: running over; abounding; exuberant; also, an inundation. Isaiah makes the overflowing flood his standing figure for an invasion that no treaty can divert.

Biblical Definition

Isaiah’s picture of judgment is water that will not respect an agreement. The rulers of Jerusalem had made a policy and boasted of it: We have made a covenant with death, and with hell are we at agreement; when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come unto us: for we have made lies our refuge, and under falsehood have we hid ourselves (Isaiah 28:15). The reply, three verses on, is that the covenant with death shall be disannulled. Men do make arrangements with what will destroy them, and they call the arrangements security. The same prophet turns the figure on the LORD Himself, and it is more frightening still: his breath, as an overflowing stream, shall reach to the midst of the neck, to sift the nations with the sieve of vanity (Isaiah 30:28). Habakkuk sees the earth’s own reaction to God in motion: The mountains saw thee, and they trembled: the overflowing of the water passed by: the deep uttered his voice, and lifted up his hands on high (Habakkuk 3:10). And Job is asked who set the channels: Who hath divided a watercourse for the overflowing of waters, or a way for the lightning of thunder? (Job 38:25) — even the flood runs where it is told.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines OVERFLOWING as running over, as a fluid; inundating; abounding; exuberant; and as a noun, an inundation, exuberance, or copiousness.

expand to see more

OVERFLOW, v.t. — To spread over, as water; to inundate; to cover with water or other fluid.

To fill beyond the brim; to run over.

OVERFLOWING, ppr. — Spreading over, as a fluid; inundating; abounding.

OVERFLOWING, n. — An inundation; exuberance; copiousness; superabundance.

From over and flow, Anglo-Saxon oferflowan.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 28:15 — "Because ye have said, We have made a covenant with death, and with hell are we at agreement; when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come unto us: for we have made lies our refuge, and under falsehood have we hid ourselves:"

Isaiah 30:28 — "And his breath, as an overflowing stream, shall reach to the midst of the neck, to sift the nations with the sieve of vanity: and there shall be a bridle in the jaws of the people, causing them to err."

Habakkuk 3:10 — "The mountains saw thee, and they trembled: the overflowing of the water passed by: the deep uttered his voice, and lifted up his hands on high."

Job 38:25 — "Who hath divided a watercourse for the overflowing of waters, or a way for the lightning of thunder;"

Modern Corruption

Isaiah 28:15 describes men sheltering under a refuge of lies and calling it prudence, which is the exact structure of every false assurance, religious or political.

expand to see more

We have made lies our refuge, and under falsehood have we hid ourselves. The rulers of Judah had not abandoned religion; they had arranged a policy — probably the Egyptian alliance — and taught themselves to regard it as safety. The phrase is one of the most useful in Scripture for exposing false assurance, because it names the mechanism: a man does not usually choose a lie knowing it to be one, he takes shelter in it and then defends the shelter. The Reformed doctrine of assurance is deliberately built against this. Assurance rests on the promises of God, the inward evidences of grace, and the testimony of the Spirit — not on a decision recorded, a ceremony undergone, or an alliance secured. The 1689 Confession warns that a man may deceive himself with false hopes and carnal presumptions, which is Isaiah 28 in confessional prose.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the same water which is judgment to the covenant-breaker is providence under God’s hand throughout. Job 38:25 asks who divided a watercourse for the overflowing of waters, and the expected answer governs everything: the flood does not escape God’s appointment, it runs in the channel He cut. Habakkuk sees the deep itself lift up its hands. Nothing in Scripture is a force loose from His government, which is why the believer under a rising flood is not being visited by chaos but is in the hands of the One who set the watercourse.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shataph (H7857), to overflow, to rinse or overwhelm; sheteph (H7858), a flood or downpour; abar (H5674), to pass over or through.

expand to see more

Hebrew shataph (H7857) — to overflow, to overwhelm; the verb behind the overflowing scourge (Isaiah 28:15).

Hebrew sheteph (H7858) — a flood, an outpouring; the overflowing of waters (Job 38:25).

Hebrew nachal (H5158) — a torrent or wadi, a channel dry until the flood comes.

Hebrew abar (H5674) — to pass over or through; the scourge that shall pass through (Isaiah 28:15).

Hebrew shot (H7752) — a scourge or whip, joined to the flood image in Isaiah 28:15.

Usage

"When the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come unto us (Isaiah 28:15) — men make arrangements with what will destroy them and call it security."

"His breath, as an overflowing stream (Isaiah 30:28) — the figure turned upon the LORD Himself."

"Who hath divided a watercourse for the overflowing of waters? (Job 38:25) — even the flood runs where it is told."
